title: OVHcloud Raises Prices as AI Memory Demand Reprices Non-AI Infrastructure
gist: OVHcloud is raising prices across most of its catalog this autumn because the AI buildout has pulled RAM fabrication capacity toward high-bandwidth memory, driving its own memory purchase index to 6x June-2025 levels with 9x expected by September 2026 and 12x forecast for early 2027. Amazon, buying the same components years ahead and designing its own accelerators, has repriced almost nothing outside reserved GPU capacity, exposing a procurement-scale asymmetry that erodes OVHcloud's price advantage from 3x cheaper to 2x cheaper. Founder Octave Klaba says the squeeze lasts until 2028, which is beyond the horizon of the European sovereign-cloud migration budgets being written now.

insights.claim: Three global RAM suppliers have reconfigured factories toward high-bandwidth memory that serves GPUs and carries better margins, at the expense of standard DDR4 and DDR5 output.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The memory shortage is a deliberate margin-driven capacity reallocation, not a demand blip, so commodity DRAM pricing stays dislocated as long as HBM economics hold.
insights.locator: Klaba set out the mechanism in a post on X

insights.claim: Indexed to June 2025, OVHcloud's own purchasing shows memory reaching 604 by June 2026, SSDs at 323, and hard drives at 148.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A real buyer's invoice index quantifies the squeeze across the whole storage stack, giving a hard input-cost benchmark for anyone modelling hosting or on-prem refresh budgets.
insights.locator: The numbers come from OVHcloud's own purchasing

insights.claim: OVHcloud's founder forecasts RAM at 9x June-2025 prices by September 2026 and 12x by early 2027, meaning the cost curve is expected to steepen rather than plateau.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Forward memory pricing implies further rounds of infrastructure repricing already committed, so current hosting quotes understate 2027 run-rate costs.
insights.quote: This month, in June 2026, we're paying 6x the price for RAM that we paid in June 2025. We already know it will be x9 in September 2026, while forecasts for early 2027 are at x12!?
insights.locator: This month, in June 2026, we're

insights.claim: The inflation extends past memory: NVMe drives are at 7x, hard drives at 3.5x, and CPUs, motherboards, and network cards are reported to be rising 15 to 20 percent.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Cost pressure is broadening across the whole bill of materials for a server, so substitution away from RAM offers no escape route.
insights.locator: He adds that NVMe drives are at 7x

insights.claim: The squeeze is framed as an exceptional condition lasting until 2028, driven by AI demand across datacenters, GPUs, token-as-a-service, and agentic AI.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A stated multi-year duration turns a one-off pricing event into a planning assumption for any capex or hosting contract signed before 2028.
insights.quote: The situation is exceptional and will last until 2028. AI demand is insane at every level: datacenters, GPUs, token-as-a-service, agentic AI.
insights.locator: Klaba is direct about how long this lasts

insights.claim: Renters of 2026-edition gaming servers face an 87 percent increase from September while other recent servers rise 40 to 59 percent, so the pain concentrates on the newest hardware generations.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Newer-generation capacity carries the repricing risk, which changes the calculus of refreshing to latest-gen hosted hardware.
insights.locator: The increases land unevenly

insights.claim: Customers on 2024-era equipment see renewal increases three to six times lower than a new order, and older ranges including Kimsufi, Rise, and earlier Advance and Scale generations are untouched.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Sitting on older fleet generations is now a material cost hedge, inverting the usual incentive to migrate to newer instance families.
insights.locator: Customers on 2024-era equipment see smaller increases

insights.claim: From October 1 storage and IP addresses become separate line items on Gen3 instances at €0.000146 per GB per hour and €0.0027 per hour, raising effective cost through unbundling rather than headline rates.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Part of the increase is hidden in restructuring, so headline price comparisons will understate the real move.
insights.locator: Some charges are also being restructured

insights.claim: OVHcloud is dropping its one-month, six-month, and 24-month saving plans while keeping the 12- and 36-month options that lock pricing for their duration.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Pruning the commitment ladder to only long lock-ins signals the provider expects costs to keep climbing and wants customers priced accordingly.
insights.locator: OVHcloud is dropping its one-month

insights.claim: Absorbing the component costs was rejected because the stated risk was running out of parts and being unable to deliver cloud capacity at all.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Supply availability, not margin defense, is the stated driver — implying physical capacity constraints may bind before price does.
insights.quote: The main concern we want to avoid is running out of parts and not being able to deliver the Cloud to you.
insights.locator: He is equally direct that absorbing the costs

insights.claim: OVHcloud buys components month by month over 12 months with no guaranteed purchase price and no visibility into real customer demand, leaving it fully exposed to spot component inflation.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Rolling merchant procurement is the structural vulnerability that separates winners from losers in a component shock, and it is visible in advance from balance-sheet and contracting behavior.
insights.quote: month by month, over 12 months, with no guarantee of the purchase price and without knowing what will be the real demand from our customers
insights.locator: Klaba described OVHcloud's purchasing position

insights.claim: Amazon buys in the same component market but has moved almost nothing, raising only EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML by roughly 20 percent in July after about 15 percent in January and leaving the rest of the catalog alone.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The same input shock produces opposite pricing behavior at hyperscalers, so component inflation is a share-shift catalyst toward the largest buyers rather than a uniform industry tax.
insights.locator: Amazon buys in the same market

insights.claim: Amazon left instances running Trainium, the accelerator it designs itself, untouched by the increase, and published the Capacity Blocks change on the pricing page with no announcement.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Vertical integration into custom silicon is showing up directly as pricing insulation, strengthening the case for in-house accelerator programs.
insights.locator: including instances running Trainium

insights.claim: Hyperscalers contract for memory years ahead in volumes that earn priority allocation, so a provider buying merchant components on rolling monthly orders has neither a pricing cushion nor supply priority.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Scale in procurement is now a durable competitive moat in commodity compute, compressing the viability of sub-scale independent cloud providers.
insights.locator: Procurement scale and vertical integration explain the gap

insights.claim: The advantage may be temporal rather than permanent: a mid-sized managed service provider founder expects Azure and AWS to announce similar increases before long, and Klaba hedges his own claims on competitors not raising prices.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: If hyperscaler forward contracts roll off into the elevated market, broad cloud price inflation becomes a 2027-2028 cost line for every enterprise IT budget.
insights.quote: if our competitors don't increase their prices
insights.locator: That gap may prove temporal rather than permanent

insights.claim: Customer complaints centered less on the size of the increase than on its frequency, coming just months after an April increase.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Repricing cadence, not level, is what breaks customer trust and triggers churn evaluations — a leading indicator of retention risk.
insights.quote: Not happy about this, especially after just raising the prices in April.
insights.locator: Customer reaction on Reddit was limited but pointed

insights.claim: Two price rises inside six months turn capacity planning into a rolling negotiation, and at least one commenter described leaving entirely for self-hosted hardware.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Cloud cost volatility is pushing marginal workloads back toward self-hosting, a reversal of the decade-long outsourcing trend worth watching in hardware demand.
insights.locator: If those reactions are representative

insights.claim: The companies driving memory demand are also the ones insulated from the resulting prices because they bought ahead of the move, creating a structural dependency for European providers.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: AI demand functions as a cost transfer from non-AI infrastructure to the AI buildout's own sponsors, compounding the incumbency advantage.
insights.quote: OVHcloud's invoices go out from Roubaix in euros, but the numbers on them are decided in fabs and purchasing departments Europe has no part in.
insights.locator: Andrei Nutas, who is serializing a book

insights.claim: The price rise cuts OVHcloud's bare metal and public cloud cost advantage from roughly 3x cheaper to 2x cheaper, conditional on competitors holding their own prices.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A quantified erosion of the discount narrows the economic case that has been carrying sovereign-cloud migrations alongside jurisdictional arguments.
insights.quote: where before we could be 3x cheaper, we will be 2x cheaper (if our competitors don't increase their prices)
insights.locator: Klaba maintains OVHcloud is still the cheapest option

insights.claim: European procurement frameworks and certification schemes increasingly favor sovereign providers on jurisdictional grounds, with cheap infrastructure doing quiet work in the underlying business cases.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Sovereignty mandates have been subsidized by a price gap that is now closing, exposing the real cost of European cloud independence.
insights.locator: That erosion matters for public sector migration

insights.claim: Airbus made protection from non-European extraterritorial law a scored criterion in its cloud tender alongside technical capability and operational excellence, but nothing in that scorecard accounts for a supplier whose input costs are set by the buying decisions of its competitors.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Sovereignty scorecards omit supply-chain cost dependency, meaning tender-driven migrations may be underwriting a structurally disadvantaged cost base.
insights.locator: As InfoQ reported, Airbus made protection

insights.claim: Elevated component prices through 2028 sit beyond the horizon of most European migration programs now running, so budgets written during the shock will outlast the shock itself.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Memory markets are cyclical and will normalize, but multi-year procurement commitments locked in at peak input costs create a lasting drag on European cloud economics.
insights.quote: Memory markets are cyclical and have crashed as sharply as they have spiked, so the shock will pass. The budgets written during it will not.
insights.locator: Timing compounds the problem
